pages.c09-p01: Describe the main features of an integrated development environment (IDE), including the editor, preferences, compiler and debugging tools
pages.c09-p02: Explain the process of translation and the differences between assemblers, compilers and interpreters
pages.c09-p03: Explain the terms syntax, data type and variable, and use the data types integer, real, character, string and Boolean appropriately
pages.c09-p04: Explain the use of variables and constants, and declare, initialise and assign them in a high-level language
pages.c09-p05: Use arithmetic, relational and Boolean (logical) operators, including integer division and modulus, and evaluate conditions
pages.c09-p06: Write programs that take input from the user, convert it to a suitable type and produce formatted output
pages.c09-p07: Describe the fundamental programming concepts of sequence, selection and iteration
pages.c09-p08: Use if, if…else, else if, nested if and switch statements for selection, with conditions built from relational and Boolean operators
pages.c09-p09: Describe count-controlled iteration and use for loops, including loops that count up, down and in steps
pages.c09-p10: Describe condition-controlled iteration and use while (pre-condition) and do…while (post-condition) loops, including sentinel values
pages.c09-p11: Use nested loops and nested selection, and trace programs that combine all three constructs
pages.c09-p12: Explain what is meant by a subroutine and describe the difference between a procedure and a function
pages.c09-p13: Write and call procedures and functions in a high-level language, using parameters, arguments and return values
pages.c09-p14: Explain passing parameters by value and by reference, and predict the effect of each
pages.c09-p15: Explain the scope of local and global variables and the advantages of using local variables
pages.c09-p16: Explain the benefits of modular programming and decomposing a problem into subroutines
pages.c09-p17: Describe the purpose of data structures and distinguish between static and dynamic structures
pages.c09-p18: Use one-dimensional and two-dimensional arrays, including traversing them with loops
pages.c09-p19: Use lists as dynamic data structures and justify the choice of a list or an array
pages.c09-p20: Describe and use records to group related fields of different data types
pages.c09-p21: Write to, append to and read from text files, splitting delimited lines into fields
pages.c09-p22: Explain why files are needed for persistent storage and how file errors can be avoided
pages.c09-p23: Describe and use validation checks, and distinguish validation from verification
pages.c09-p24: Use exception handling to deal with run-time errors
pages.c09-p25: Explain the differences between syntax, semantic, run-time and logic errors
pages.c09-p26: Select valid, extreme, invalid and null test data and use a test plan to find errors
pages.c09-p27: Use the debugging tools of an integrated development environment (IDE), such as breakpoints, stepping and watches, to locate errors (IDE features are introduced in AP19)
pages.c09-p28: Explain how the choice of translator (compiler or interpreter, covered in AP19) affects when syntax, semantic and run-time errors are detected

q.q: A program fails to build. What happens when the programmer double-clicks an entry in the IDE's error list?
o: The IDE corrects the error automatically
The program runs up to the faulty line
The editor jumps straight to the faulty line
A breakpoint is set on the faulty line
q.why: Translation errors appear in an error list with a description and line number; double-clicking jumps to the line.

q.q: How does syntax highlighting help a programmer?
o: Invalid code is underlined with a wavy line before the program is built
Keywords and variable names are suggested after typing a few letters
Keywords, strings and comments are coloured, so structure is easier to read
Blocks that are not being worked on are collapsed to save space
q.why: Highlighting colours different parts of the code, so an unclosed string stands out. The others describe syntax checking, code completion and code folding.

q.q: Which statement about an IDE is correct?
o: Its syntax checker finds every logic error in the code as it is being typed
Its syntax checker and compiler catch syntax errors, but logic errors need testing
Its compiler finds all errors, so a program that builds will give correct results
Its debugging tools fix run-time errors automatically once they are located
q.why: An IDE does not find all errors: logic errors are only found by testing and debugging.

q.q: Why is assembly language used for device drivers and embedded systems?
o: It runs on any processor without change, so drivers work on every machine
It is tied to one processor family and gives precise control of the hardware
It is translated line by line, so errors are reported as soon as they occur
It hides the hardware from the programmer, which makes drivers simpler
q.why: Each mnemonic maps to one machine code instruction for a particular processor family, giving precise hardware control.

q.q: How is a C# program translated and run?
o: It is compiled to an intermediate language, which .NET compiles to machine code just in time
It is interpreted one statement at a time, with no object code ever produced
It is assembled one mnemonic to one machine code instruction before running
It is compiled directly to machine code for one processor, with no runtime
q.why: C# mixes the two ideas: compiled to intermediate language, then compiled 'just in time' by the .NET runtime. For the exam treat it as compiled.

q.q: Why can an interpreted program leave a file half-updated after an error?
o: Statements before the faulty line have already run when the error is found
Interpreters translate the whole program first, then run it all at once
Interpreters delete any file that is open when the program crashes
Interpreters cannot close files, so the last changes are never saved
q.why: An interpreter only finds an error when it reaches that line, after earlier statements have run.

q.q: Why does an interpreted program usually run more slowly than a compiled one?
o: The interpreter produces object code that must be optimised before it runs
The interpreter lists every error together before any statement can run
The interpreter translates into assembly language rather than machine code
Each statement is translated again every time it runs, even inside loops
q.why: An interpreter produces no object code, so translation is repeated on each run and on every pass of a loop.

q.q: Which data type is most suitable for storing a mobile phone number such as 07712 345678?
o: Integer
String
Real
Character
q.why: It begins with 0, may contain spaces and is never used in arithmetic, so it must be text; an integer would lose the leading zero.

q.q: Which is a valid C# char value?
o: 'MK'
"MK"
q.why: A char holds exactly one character in single quotes; double quotes make a string.

q.q: Why do C# programmers prefer decimal to double for money?
o: decimal uses less memory than double, so totals are calculated more quickly
double cannot store any value with a fractional part, such as pounds and pence
decimal rounds every value to two places automatically when it is stored
decimal stores values such as 0.10 exactly; double can introduce tiny rounding errors
q.why: double is a binary type and can introduce tiny rounding errors; decimal stores values like 0.10 exactly.

q.q: Which of these is a rule enforced by the C# compiler, rather than a naming convention?
o: Variable names should be written in camelCase
Identifiers are case-sensitive and cannot contain spaces
Constant names should be written in capital letters
Names should be meaningful, such as ticketPrice
q.why: Rules (no spaces, not a keyword, start with a letter or underscore, case-sensitive) are enforced; the others are good-practice conventions.

q.q: After int n = 5; n *= n - 2; what is the value of n?
q.why: The right-hand side is evaluated first: n - 2 = 3, then n = 5 × 3 = 15.

q.q: A program declares const decimal VAT_RATE = 0.2m; and later contains VAT_RATE = 0.25m;. What happens?
o: A run-time exception is thrown
A compile-time error is reported
The rate changes to 0.25
The new value is ignored silently
q.why: Any attempt to assign a new value to a constant is rejected by the compiler.

q.q: What does 47 % 8 evaluate to in C#?
q.why: 47 = 5 × 8 + 7, so the remainder is 7. 5 is the result of 47 / 8 (integer division).

q.q: int minutes = 135; What are the values of minutes / 60 and minutes % 60?
o: 15 and 2
2 and 15
q.why: Integer division gives the whole hours (2) and modulus gives the minutes left over (15).

q.q: Which expression is true when the int n is even?
q.why: The remainder after dividing by 2 is 0 for even numbers. n / 2 is integer division, not the remainder.

q.q: With int total = 7, count = 2; which expression gives 3.5?
o: (double)total / count
total / count
(int)(total / count)
(double)(total / count)
q.why: Casting one operand before dividing forces real division. (double)(total / count) casts after integer division has already given 3.

q.q: Which statement correctly reads a whole number of nights typed by the user?
o: int nights = Console.ReadLine();
string nights = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine());
int nights = Console.ReadLine().Length;
int nights = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine());
q.why: ReadLine returns a string, so it must be converted with int.Parse before being stored in an int.

q.q: double cost = 54.7125; is output with {cost:F2}. What is displayed and what is stored?
o: 54.71 is displayed; cost now holds 54.71
54.72 is displayed; cost still holds 54.7125
54.71 is displayed; cost still holds 54.7125
54.7125 is displayed; cost now holds 54.71
q.why: F2 rounds to two places for display only; formatting does not change the value stored.

q.q: What happens if int.Parse is given the text "12a"?
o: It returns the value 12
It returns the value 0
A FormatException is thrown at run time
The compiler reports a syntax error
q.why: The text is not a valid integer, so a run-time exception occurs.

q.q: What is output by Console.WriteLine("Total: " + 5 + 3);?
o: Total: 53
Total: 8
Total: 5 3
A compile error
q.why: Once a string is on the left, + joins text, so 5 then 3 are appended. Brackets (5 + 3) would give 8.

q.q: Which is the best description of iteration?
o: Repeating the whole program again from the start
Choosing which block of statements to run next
Repeating a specific block of statements, the loop body
Running statements one after another in order
q.why: Iteration repeats the loop body, not 'the program'. Choosing a path is selection; running in order is sequence.

q.q: A program keeps asking for a password until the user types the correct one. Which construct is most appropriate?
o: Condition-controlled iteration
Count-controlled iteration
Selection only
Sequence only
q.why: The number of attempts is not known in advance, so the loop must repeat while a condition holds.

q.q: Why does the order of statements in a sequence matter?
o: The compiler always reorders statements, so the order written has no effect on the output
Later statements depend on results of earlier ones, so changing the order can change the output
Only the first statement in a sequence runs; the rest are skipped unless a loop is used
Statements in a sequence run at the same time, so their order only affects the speed
q.why: For example, a total must be calculated after the values are input and before it is output.

q.q: In the chain if (points >= 90) Gold; else if (points >= 75) Silver; else if (points >= 50) Bronze; else Participation, what is the award for 75?
o: Gold
Bronze
Silver and Bronze
Silver
q.why: 75 >= 90 is false, 75 >= 75 is true, so Silver is assigned and the rest of the chain is skipped.

q.q: Awards are set with three separate if statements (not else if): points >= 90 Gold, points >= 75 Silver, points >= 50 Bronze. What award does 95 end with?
o: Gold
Silver
Participation
Bronze
q.why: With separate ifs, every true condition runs, so Gold is overwritten by Silver and then by Bronze.

q.q: A ticket machine first checks whether a passenger has a Smartpass and, only if not, checks the time of day for an off-peak fare. Which structure is this?
o: Nested selection
A switch statement
A count-controlled loop
A sentinel-controlled loop
q.why: Nested selection puts one if inside another, so the inner decision is only made for one outcome of the outer one.

q.q: Which condition correctly tests whether a fridge reading is outside the safe range 2 to 8 inclusive?
o: temp < 2 && temp > 8
temp <= 2 || temp >= 8
temp < 2 || temp > 8
temp > 2 && temp < 8
q.why: Outside means below 2 OR above 8. No value can be both, so && is never true; <= and >= wrongly include 2 and 8.

q.q: How many passes does for (int i = 10; i >= 0; i -= 5) make?
q.why: i takes 10, 5 and 0; the next value, -5, fails the condition.

q.q: Why should a for loop's counter not be changed inside the loop body?
o: The number of passes becomes hard to predict, a common cause of logic errors
The compiler rejects any assignment to a loop counter inside the body
The loop body will then run exactly once, whatever the condition is
The counter would become a global variable visible in every subroutine
q.why: Changing the counter in the body makes the number of passes hard to predict and is a frequent source of logic errors.

q.q: When is the condition of a C# for loop tested?
o: After every pass
Before every pass
Only once, at the start
Only when the counter changes
q.why: It is a pre-test: if false initially, the body never runs. The update runs after every pass.

q.q: What is the last value output by for (int i = 2; i < 15; i += 3) Console.WriteLine(i);?
q.why: i takes 2, 5, 8, 11, 14; the next value, 17, fails i < 15.

q.q: Why is a do…while loop well suited to validating input?
o: The user must be asked at least once, and the test comes after the body
The condition is tested before the body, so invalid data is never read
It repeats a fixed number of times known before the loop starts
It cannot become an infinite loop, whatever the user types in
q.why: A post-condition loop always runs at least once, which suits menus and input validation.

q.q: A sentinel loop totals values until -1 is entered. The inputs are 8000, 6500, 9100, -1. What is the total?
q.why: The sentinel -1 is not data, so total = 8000 + 6500 + 9100 = 23 600.

q.q: A REPEAT … UNTIL score >= 50 loop is rewritten in C#. Which is correct?
o: do { … } while (score >= 50);
while (score >= 50) { … }
do { … } while (score > 50);
do { … } while (score < 50);
q.why: UNTIL stops when its condition becomes true, so do…while must continue while it is false: the condition is reversed.

q.q: In the steps program, the user types -1 as the very first value. What happens?
o: The loop runs once and the average is shown as -1
The loop body never runs, and 'No data entered' is output
The program crashes with a division by zero error
The loop runs forever because count stays at 0
q.why: A while loop tests first, so the body is skipped; the count > 0 guard prevents dividing by zero.

q.q: count starts at 0. for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) contains for (int j = 1; j <= 3; j++) count++; What is count at the end?
q.why: The inner loop runs completely for each outer pass: 4 × 3 = 12.

q.q: for (int row = 1; row <= 3; row++) contains for (int col = 1; col <= row; col++) which outputs one star each pass. How many stars are output altogether?
q.why: The inner limit depends on row: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 stars.

q.q: In the star program, the inner header is changed to for (int col = 1; col < row; col++). What is output on the third line?
o: Nothing
q.why: With row = 3, col takes only 1 and 2, so two stars.

q.q: When tracing combined code in a trace table, when should a new row be added?
o: Whenever a value changes, following the code exactly as written
Once for each line of code, whether or not anything changes
Only at the end of each pass of the outermost loop
Only when the program produces some output
q.why: A new row is added whenever a value changes, working through the code statement by statement as the computer would.

q.q: When a called subroutine finishes, where does control return to?
o: The statement immediately after the call
The first statement of the main program
The last statement of the main program
The first statement of the subroutine
q.why: Control passes to the subroutine and returns to the statement after the call when it ends.

q.q: How is a procedure call normally written, compared with a function call?
o: A function call is a statement on its own; a procedure call is used inside an expression
Both are always written inside an expression so that a value can be stored
A procedure call needs the keyword void; a function call needs the keyword return
A procedure call is a statement on its own; a function call is used inside an expression
q.why: ShowMenu(); stands alone, while double t = AddVat(40); uses the returned value.

q.q: Console.WriteLine, Math.Round and int.Parse are examples of...
o: user-defined procedures
global variables
library routines
local functions
q.why: Library routines are prewritten subroutines supplied with the language and already tested.

q.q: What is a subroutine's interface?
o: Its name, parameters and return type
The code inside the subroutine's body
The local variables it declares
The list of places it is called from
q.why: A clear interface lets other programmers use the subroutine without reading the code inside it.

q.q: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
o: An argument is named in the subroutine header; a parameter is the value supplied in the call
A parameter is used only by functions; an argument is used only by procedures
A parameter is a global variable; an argument is a local variable in the subroutine
A parameter is named in the subroutine header; an argument is the value supplied in the call
q.why: The parameter is in the definition; the argument is in the call.

q.q: MonthlyFee(int age, bool offPeak) sets fee to 20.00 if age < 18, otherwise 36.00, then multiplies by 0.75 if offPeak. What does MonthlyFee(42, true) return?
q.why: 42 is not under 18, so fee = 36.00; off-peak gives 36.00 × 0.75 = 27.00.

q.q: A function has one path through an if statement that does not reach a return statement. What happens?
o: The function returns 0 on that path
A run-time exception occurs
The compiler reports an error
The function returns null on that path
q.why: Every path through a function must reach a return, or the compiler reports an error.

q.q: How is passing by reference requested in C#?
o: With ref in the header only
With ref in both the header and the call
With ref in the call only
It is the default, so nothing is needed
q.why: C# needs ref in both places, which makes the intention obvious. By value is the default.

q.q: int score = 25; AddBonusByRef(ref score); where the parameter is ref int points and the method adds 10 to points. What is score afterwards?
q.why: By reference, the parameter refers to the original variable, so score itself becomes 35.

q.q: int.TryParse(text, out n) uses an out parameter. What does this allow the method to do?
o: Convert the text without needing any variable to store it
Throw an exception if the text is not a valid integer
Pass a copy of n so that the caller's n is protected
Return a success flag and also give back the converted number
q.why: out is a variant of by reference: the method must assign n, so it can give back more than one result.

q.q: What is a disadvantage of passing by reference?
o: The subroutine is not able to read the value that has been passed in
It always uses more memory than passing a copy of the value
It cannot be used with integer variables, only with strings
Unintended changes to the caller's variables can make errors hard to trace
q.why: Side effects leak back to the caller. Copying large data is the drawback of passing by value.

q.q: A subroutine declares a local variable with the same name as a global variable and changes it. What happens to the global?
o: It changes too, because both names refer to the same memory location
It is unchanged, because the local hides the global inside that subroutine
It is deleted when the subroutine ends, along with the local variable
The compiler rejects the program because the two names are the same
q.why: Inside the subroutine the local hides the global; changing the local does not change the global.

q.q: Which is an advantage of using local variables?
o: Their values are kept between calls so totals build up automatically
The same name can be reused in different subroutines without interference
They can be accessed from anywhere in the program for the whole run
They hold their memory for the whole run, so they are always available
q.why: Locals are self-contained, so names like count can be reused safely. The other options describe globals.

q.q: A subroutine is called three times. What happens to its local variable between calls?
o: It keeps its last value for the next call
It is destroyed and created afresh on the next call
It becomes a global variable after the first call
It is saved to a file until the next call
q.why: Locals exist only while their subroutine runs, so their value does not carry over.

q.q: LogVisit(int adults) declares local int bonusPoints = adults * 5 and adds it to the global-style field Club.totalPoints, which starts at 0. After LogVisit(3); LogVisit(4); what is Club.totalPoints?
q.why: The first call adds 3 × 5 = 15 and the second adds 4 × 5 = 20, giving 35. Each call creates a fresh bonusPoints.

q.q: Why is integration testing still needed when every module has been tested on its own?
o: Modules tested on their own are never compiled, so they must be tested again
Each module must be rewritten into one large program before it can be released
Integration testing is the only way to find syntax errors in separate modules
Modules can work alone yet fail when combined, e.g. one uses pence and another pounds
q.why: Modules must be tested together because interfaces may not match, as in the pence/pounds example.

q.q: Why must agreed interfaces be in place before a team builds modules in parallel?
o: So that global variables can be shared freely between all of the modules
So that no integration testing is needed once the modules are finished
So that modules written separately fit together correctly when integrated
So that the compiler can translate each module more quickly
q.why: Each programmer relies on agreed names, parameters and return types.

q.q: TicketCost(int n) multiplies n by £8.50 and applies a 10% discount if n >= 6. What does TicketCost(6) return?
q.why: 6 × £8.50 = £51.00; the 10% group discount gives £45.90.

q.q: Which is an example of a dynamic data structure?
o: A list of bookings that grows during the day
An array of 12 monthly sales totals
A 10 × 10 two-dimensional array game board
A record with a fixed set of four fields
q.why: A dynamic structure grows and shrinks at run time; arrays are static.

q.q: Which data structure holds a fixed set of named fields of different data types describing one item?
o: A list
A one-dimensional array
A two-dimensional array
A record
q.why: Records group named fields, which can be of different types; arrays and lists hold items of one type.

q.q: Why use a data structure rather than many separate variables such as mark1, mark2, … mark30?
o: It always uses less memory than separate variables
It removes the need to choose a data type for the items
It makes the program compile more quickly
Items share one identifier, so a loop can process them all
q.why: A single identifier with an index lets a loop handle every item.

q.q: What values do the elements of new int[5] hold when it is created?
q.why: new int[5] creates five elements, each set to 0.

q.q: int[,] sold = { { 40, 55, 70 }, { 60, 80, 95 } }; Nested loops output the total of each row. What is output for Day 1?
q.why: Row 1 is 60 + 80 + 95 = 235. Row 0 totals 165.

q.q: When working out row totals of a 2D array with nested loops, where must the row total be reset to 0?
o: Inside the inner loop, before adding each value
Once, before both loops begin
Inside the outer loop, before the inner loop
After both loops have finished
q.why: Resetting inside the outer loop starts each row afresh. Resetting in the inner loop loses values; resetting once gives a running grand total.

q.q: int[] litres = { 30, 0, 45, 25, 0, 50, 10 }; A loop finds the index of the largest value. What is it?
q.why: 50 is the largest value and it is at index 5 (counting from 0).

q.q: A list n holds 4, 9, 6, 1. After n.Insert(2, 7); what is n[3]?
q.why: Insert puts 7 at index 2 and shifts later items along: 4, 9, 7, 6, 1, so n[3] is 6.

q.q: Which situation best suits a list rather than an array?
o: The 12 months of the year
The 64 squares of a chessboard
Customers joining a queue for a cash machine
The 7 days of the week
q.why: The number of customers varies; the others are fixed sizes.

q.q: What does a C# list's IndexOf method return if the item is not in the list?
o: false
null
q.why: IndexOf returns the index, or −1 if absent. Contains returns true or false.

q.q: A list rota holds Eimear, Jack, Sinead. After rota.Insert(1, "Tom"); rota.Remove("Jack"); what is rota.IndexOf("Sinead")?
q.why: Insert gives Eimear, Tom, Jack, Sinead; Remove gives Eimear, Tom, Sinead, so Sinead is at index 2.

q.q: What distinguishes a record from an array?
o: A record's fields can be of different data types
A record can only hold integer values
A record has no fixed set of fields
A record can only be stored on disk
q.why: Array elements share one type; record fields need not.

q.q: What does Player[] squad = new Player[26]; create?
o: One Player record with 26 fields
A list of Player records that can grow beyond 26
A Player record type with 26 field names
An array that can hold 26 Player records
q.why: new Player[26] creates an array of records; the record type itself must already have been declared.

q.q: In database terms, what does one record (for example, one player) correspond to?
o: A column
A table
A field
A row
q.why: A record is a row, a field is a column, and a list or array of records is a table.

q.q: A file members.csv already holds 50 lines. It is opened with new StreamWriter("members.csv", false) and one line is written. How many lines does it now hold?
q.why: false means write mode, which overwrites the file completely. true would append, giving 51.

q.q: What does "Ross,42,7.5".Split(',') return?
o: Three variables of different types
A record with three fields
The number 42
An array of three strings
q.why: Split always returns a string array; converting each field is a separate step.

q.q: In the CSV line Aisling,16,true what is the role of the comma?
o: It marks the end of the record
It is a delimiter separating the fields
It is a sentinel value ending the file
It converts the fields to text
q.why: In a CSV file each line is one record and the fields are separated by a delimiter such as a comma.

q.q: A program reads the line "Fionn,17,false" and splits it into f. Which statement correctly gets the age as a number?
o: int age = f[1];
int age = int.Parse(f[2]);
int age = int.Parse(f[1]);
int age = f.Parse(1);
q.why: Everything read from a text file is text, so the second field (index 1) must be converted with int.Parse.

q.q: A booking app exports a CSV file that is opened in a spreadsheet. Which use of files does this show?
o: Keeping a log or audit trail
Storing more data than fits in memory
Keeping data in volatile RAM
Sharing data between programs
q.why: Files let data be shared between programs, as well as kept between runs, logged, and used when too large for memory.

q.q: A program tries to read a file that is open in another program. Which exception is it most likely to meet?
o: FormatException
IndexOutOfRangeException
IOException
DivideByZeroException
q.why: A file open elsewhere or without permission gives IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException.

q.q: Why is checking File.Exists not enough on its own to avoid file errors?
o: File.Exists only works for files that have already been opened
File.Exists deletes the file if it is open in another program
File.Exists can only check files stored in the cloud, not on disk
The file could be deleted or locked between the check and the read
q.why: That is why exception handling is still needed.

q.q: A program checks that the county entered is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland. Which validation check is this?
o: Format
Range
Lookup
Presence
q.why: A lookup check confirms the value is in a list of allowed values.

q.q: A user is asked to type a new password twice. What is this?
o: Verification by double entry
A range check
A lookup check
A presence check
q.why: The two entries are compared to confirm accuracy.

q.q: A date of birth of 03/07/2009 passes every validation check but is the wrong date. Why was it accepted?
o: The range check was written with the wrong operator
Verification was used instead of validation
The format check only works on postcodes
Validation shows data is allowable, not that it is correct
q.why: Valid data can still be wrong; verification (double entry or visual check) checks accuracy.

q.q: Which check confirms that a PIN is exactly 4 characters?
o: Length
Range
Format
Type
q.why: A length check tests that the number of characters is within limits.

q.q: When does a finally block run?
o: Only if an exception occurs
Only if no exception occurs
Only when the program ends
Whether or not an exception occurs
q.why: finally always runs, making it ideal for tidying up such as closing a file.

q.q: An exception occurs on the second line of a five-line try block. What happens to lines 3 to 5 of the try block?
o: They run after the catch block
They are skipped
They run before the catch block
They run only if finally is present
q.why: Once an exception occurs, the rest of the try block is skipped and the matching catch runs.

q.q: Why is an empty catch { } that silently swallows every error poor practice?
o: The compiler rejects any catch block that contains no statements
It stops the finally block from running after the exception
The program carries on with bad data and the bug becomes harder to find
It makes the program crash instead of handling the exception
q.why: Always give a meaningful response; silent catches hide bugs.

q.q: scores = { 12, 18, 9 }. A try block reads r = 1 and players = 0, then outputs scores[r] / players. There are catches for FormatException, IndexOutOfRangeException and DivideByZeroException, and a finally block. What happens?
o: The IndexOutOfRangeException message, then 'Calculation finished.'
The DivideByZeroException message, then 'Calculation finished.'
The DivideByZeroException message only, as finally is skipped
The program crashes, because 18 / 0 cannot be caught
q.why: 18 / 0 is integer division by zero, so that catch runs; finally always runs afterwards.

q.q: A program calculates area = (length + width) * 2 instead of length * width. It runs without any message. Which type of error is this?
o: Logic
Syntax
Semantic
Run-time
q.why: It runs normally but produces the wrong result, with no error message.

q.q: Which error is reported by the compiler and stops the program being built?
o: Division by zero
An off-by-one error
A missing semicolon
A wrong formula
q.why: A missing semicolon is a syntax error, which prevents compilation.

q.q: Which line contains a syntax error?
o: int total = 0;
whlie (x > 0)
q.why: A misspelt keyword breaks the grammar of the language, so the program will not compile.

q.q: int age = "sixteen"; is grammatically correct C# but has no valid meaning. Which type of error is it?
o: Syntax
Logic
Semantic
Run-time
q.why: Semantic errors are grammatical but meaningless; C# catches many, like this type mismatch, at compile time.

q.q: Ages from 0 to 120 are accepted, with a concession from 65. Which value is invalid test data?
q.why: 121 is outside the allowed range. 0, 120 and 65 are extreme (boundary) data, which is still valid.

q.q: Why must both sides of every boundary be tested?
o: Boundary values are the only data the program will receive in real use
Normal data always reveals errors, so boundaries are tested only for speed
A wrong relational operator only affects the value exactly on the boundary
Boundary tests are needed only to find syntax errors before compiling
q.why: Using > instead of >= changes only the boundary value, so normal data alone would never reveal it.

q.q: Which set of columns belongs in a test plan?
o: Variable names, condition, output and one row for each value change
Who changed the code, when it was changed and a note on the change
Task, depends on, duration, earliest start and earliest finish
Purpose, test data, type of data, expected outcome, actual outcome, pass/fail
q.why: These are the test plan columns. The others describe a trace table, a version history and a task table.

q.q: What does 'step out' do in the IDE's debugger?
o: Executes the next line and enters any subroutine it calls
Executes the next line, running any call as a single step
Runs the rest of the current subroutine and pauses after the call
Shows the chain of calls that led to the current line
q.why: Step out leaves a subroutine quickly once you have seen enough. The others describe step into, step over and the call stack.

q.q: An exception is thrown inside a subroutine called from three places. Which tool shows which caller was involved?
o: Call stack
Watch window
Step out
Breakpoint
q.why: The call stack lists the chain of calls that led to the current line.

q.q: How does debugging differ from testing?
o: Testing shows that something is wrong; debugging finds where and why
Debugging shows that something is wrong; testing finds where and why
Debugging tools fix the errors automatically, so testing is not needed
Testing finds only syntax errors; debugging finds only logic errors
q.why: Debugging tools do not fix errors and are no substitute for a test plan.

q.q: A syntax error lies in a rarely used branch of a C# program. When is it found?
o: Only when that branch is executed, possibly weeks after release
Only when a test plan includes data that reaches that branch
Never, because syntax errors in branches are ignored by compilers
Before the program runs, listed together with any other syntax errors
q.why: A compiler translates the whole program, so a program that builds has no syntax errors, even in rarely used branches.

q.q: An interpreted program updates 50 records then hits a syntax error in line 80. What is the risk?
o: None, because the interpreter undoes the changes
The error is reported before line 1 runs
The data may be left half-updated
The records are rolled back automatically
q.why: Earlier statements have already executed when the interpreter reaches the faulty line.

q.q: In a strongly typed compiled language such as C#, when are most semantic errors, such as type mismatches, detected?
o: Only when the statement is executed
Only during acceptance testing
At compile time, before the program runs
Never, as they are legal code
q.why: C#'s compiler catches most semantic errors; with an interpreter they are usually found only when the statement runs.
